passage: Daycare note, Tuesday Jagdish, two, screamed and dropped to the floor when the hand dryer roared in the washroom. He covered his ears and would not go back in. At sand play he pulled his hands out as if the sand burned. What I did: we now use paper towels with him, and the dryer stays off when he is inside. I put dry rice in a small tub; he watched, then poked one finger in. We will not force the sand. - Swati, caregiver

qa.q: What does the daycare now use with Jagdish instead of the dryer?
How can you tell the hand dryer upset Jagdish?
qa.a: He was frightened and overwhelmed by the noise: he screamed, dropped to the floor, covered his ears and would not go back in.

qa.q: Which choice by Swati was gentle rather than forceful?
qa.a: Swati offered a small tub of dry rice and let him poke one finger in, without forcing the sand.

qa.q: How might the other children's day change because of these small adjustments?
qa.a: The room would likely stay calmer, since Jagdish is not screaming in the washroom and can join play his own way.

grounding: A caregiver's note on a toddler who screams at hand dryers and refuses a texture, using a calm setup and gentle exposure instead of force.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Harsha spins and spins until she tumbles into the hay, laughing. Then she climbs up and crashes into the hay again. At dinner she bumps her head against her mother Reena's arm, hard, over and over. The neighbours say, "Stop her, she'll get wild." Reena does not scold. She ties a sack swing to the neem tree. Harsha swings, stomach down, for a long time. Afterwards she sits quietly in Reena's lap and eats her roti.

qa.q: What does Reena tie to the neem tree?
What does Harsha sitting quietly in Reena's lap after swinging suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels calmer and settled once her body has had enough movement.

qa.q: Which choice by Reena worked better than scolding?
qa.a: She gave Harsha a safe swing for the spinning and crashing her body wanted, instead of stopping her.

qa.q: How do the neighbours see Harsha's spinning differently from Reena?
qa.a: The neighbours see it as wildness to stop, while Reena seems to see a need her daughter's body has.

grounding: It shows a toddler who seeks spinning and crashing, and a mother who offers a calmer, safe outlet instead of force.
